'''Ivar Giaever'''{{Efn|{{IPAc-en|ˈ|j|eɪ|v|ər}} {{Respell|YAY|ver}};<ref>{{Cite dictionary |title=Giaever|url=https://www.dictionary.com/browse/giaever|url-status=live |dictionary=Dictionary.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240301082815/https://www.dictionary.com/browse/giaever|archive-date=2024-03-01|access-date=2025-06-24}}</ref> {{Langx|no|Giæver}}, {{IPA|no|ˈjæːvər|pron}}}} (April 5, 1929 – June 20, 2025) was a Norwegian–American [[physicist]] who shared the 1973 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] with [[Leo Esaki]] and [[Brian Josephson]]. One half of the prize was jointly awarded to Esaki and Giaever "for their experimental discoveries regarding [[Quantum tunneling|tunneling]] phenomena in [[semiconductor]]s and [[superconductor]]s, respectively."<ref name="Nobel Prize">{{Cite web|title=Nobel Prize in Physics 1973|url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1973/summary/|url-status=live|publisher=NobelPrize.org|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110621141041/http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/1973/index.html |archive-date=2011-06-21|access-date=2008-10-09}}</ref>

== Biography ==
Ivar Giaever was born on April 5, 1929, in [[Bergen]], Norway, the second of three children of John A. Giaever, a pharmacist. He grew up in [[Toten]], where he attended elementary school, before moving to [[Hamar]] to receive his secondary education. In 1948, Giaever entered the [[Norwegian Institute of Technology]] (now part of the [[Norwegian University of Science and Technology]]), where he graduated in 1952 with a degree in Mechanical Engineering. In 1953, he completed his military service in the [[Norwegian Army]], before going on to work for the [[Norwegian Patent Office]] as a patent examiner.<ref name="Nobel bio"/>

In 1954, Giaever emigrated to Canada to join the Advanced Engineering Program of [[Canadian General Electric]]. He then moved to the United States in 1956, and worked as an applied mathematician for [[General Electric]] until 1958, when he became a researcher at the [[General Electric Research Laboratory]].<ref name="Nobel bio">{{Cite web|title=Ivar Giaever – Biographical|url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1973/giaever/biographical/|url-status=live|publisher=NobelPrize.org|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101214232747/http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/1973/giaever-bio.html|archive-date=2010-12-14|access-date=2011-06-27}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Giaever, Ivar |url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11511002.html|url-status=dead|publisher=American Institute of Physics|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241207213323/https://history.aip.org/phn/11511002.html|archive-date=2024-12-07|access-date=2025-07-04}}</ref> 

In 1964, Giaever received a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] in Theoretical Physics from [[Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute]], where he was an Institute Professor from 1988 until his retirement in 2004.<ref name="Rensselaer">{{Cite web|title=Giaever, Ivar, 1929-|url=https://guides.archives.rpi.edu/agents/people/1406|publisher=Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute |access-date=November 3, 2026}}</ref> He was also a professor at the [[University of Oslo]], sponsored by [[Statoil]].<ref name="Nobel bio"/>

Giaever died on June 20, 2025, in [[Schenectady, New York]], at the age of 96. He is buried in the cemetery of [[Hoff Church]] in [[Østre Toten]], Norway.<ref>{{Cite newspaper|title=Nobelpris-vinner Ivar Giæver er død |url=https://www.vg.no/nyheter/i/0VadK6/nobelpris-vinner-ivar-giaever-er-doed|newspaper=Verdens Gang|language=no|date=2025-07-03|access-date=2025-07-03}}</ref>

== Research ==
=== Tunneling ===
From 1958 to 1969, Giaever worked on [[thin film]]s, [[Quantum tunnelling|tunneling]], and [[superconductivity]].<ref name="Nobel bio"/> In 1960, following from [[Leo Esaki]]'s discovery of tunneling in [[semiconductor]]s in 1957, Giaever showed that tunneling also took place in [[superconductor]]s, demonstrating tunneling through a very thin layer of [[oxide]] surrounded on both sides by metal in a superconducting or normal state.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Giaever|first=Ivar| year=1960|title=Energy Gap in Superconductors Measured by Electron Tunneling|url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.5.147|url-access=subscription|journal=[[Physical Review Letters]]|volume=5|issue=4|pages=147–148|bibcode=1960PhRvL...5..147G| doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.5.147}}</ref> His experiments demonstrated the existence of an [[energy gap]] in superconductors, one of the most important predictions of the [[BCS theory]] of superconductivity, which had been developed in 1957.{{Efn|[[John Bardeen|Bardeen]], [[Leon Cooper|Cooper]], and [[John Robert Schrieffer|Schrieffer]] won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1972 for this theoretical advance, which bears their initials.}} Giaever's experimental demonstration of tunneling in superconductors stimulated the theoretical physicist [[Brian Josephson]] to work on the phenomenon, leading to his prediction of the [[Josephson effect]] in 1962. Esaki and Giaever shared half of the 1973 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]], and Josephson received the other half.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Press release: 1973 Nobel Prize in Physics |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1973/press-release/|url-status=live |publisher=NobelPrize.org|date=1973-10-23 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110517091855/http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/1973/press.html|archive-date=2011-05-17|access-date=2011-06-27}}</ref>

=== Biophysics ===
Giaever's research later in his career was mainly in the field of [[biophysics]]. In 1969, he was awarded a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] to study biophysics for one year at the [[University of Cambridge]] in England.<ref name="Nobel bio"/> In 1991, Giaever and Charles R. Keese (who worked with Giaever at GE) founded Applied BioPhysics Inc., a company that develops and markets [[electric cell-substrate impedance sensing]].<ref name="Rensselaer"/>

== Activism ==
Giaever was a [[climate change denier]], who fueled doubt on [[climate change]],<ref>{{Cite magazine|last1=Corbin|first1=Jeffrey D.|last2=Katz|first2=Miriam E.|date=2012-07-03|title=Effective strategies to counter campus presentations on climate denial|url=https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2012EO270007|magazine=[[Eos (magazine)|Eos]]|doi=10.1029/2012EO270007}}</ref> for example calling it a "new religion." However, he had presented no strong evidence to support this position.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Strassel|first=Kimberley A.|date=2009-06-26|title=The Climate Change Climate Change|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB124597505076157449|url-access=subscription|url-status=live|newspaper=[[The Wall Street Journal]]|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110704010453/http://online.wsj.com/article/SB124597505076157449.html|archive-date=2011-07-04|access-date=2011-06-26}}</ref> On September 13, 2011, he resigned from the [[American Physical Society]], after the organization called the evidence of damaging global warming "incontrovertible."<ref>{{Cite news|last=Sherwell|first=Philip|date=2011-09-25|title=War of words over global warming as Nobel laureate resigns in protest|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/earth/environment/climatechange/8786565/War-of-words-over-global-warming-as-Nobel-laureate-resigns-in-protest.html|url-access=subscription|newspaper=[[The Daily Telegraph|The Telegraph]]}}</ref>

Giaever was a science advisor to the [[Heartland Institute]], an American conservative and libertarian [[think tank]] that denies climate change.<ref>{{cite web|title=Ivar Giaever|url=https://www.heartland.org/about-us/who-we-are/ivar-giaever|website=www.heartland.org|access-date=June 9, 2017}}</ref>

Giaever co-signed a letter from over 70 Nobel laureate scientists to the [[Louisiana State Legislature]] supporting the repeal of the anti-evolution [[Louisiana Science Education Act]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=77 Nobel Laureates Call for a Repeal of the LSEA|url=http://www.repealcreationism.com/397/nobellaureateletter/|url-status=dead|website=www.repealcreationism.com|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120920132926/http://www.repealcreationism.com/397/nobellaureateletter/|archive-date=2012-09-20|access-date=2012-01-15}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
In 1952, Giaever married his childhood sweetheart, Inger Skramstad, who died on September 12, 2023, at the age of 94. They had four children.<ref>{{Cite newspaper|title=Inger Giaever Obituary|url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/dailygazette/name/inger-giaever-obituary?id=53176674|date=2023-09-24|newspaper=[[The Daily Gazette]]|access-date=2024-05-19}}</ref>

In 1964, Giaever became a [[naturalized U.S. citizen]].<ref name="Nobel bio"/>

Giaever was an [[atheist]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Giaever|first=Ivar|date=November 2016|title="I Am The Smartest Man I Know": A Nobel Laureate's Difficult Journey|publisher=World Scientific|isbn=978-981-3109-17-9}}</ref>
